title: the Rajasuya
hook: Yudhishthira wants to give the sacrifice up; Bhima and Arjuna argue for it, and Krishna tells how Jarasandha was born in two halves

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rajasuya ran into a locked gate: Jarasandha of Magadha, and the kings in his prison. What stood in the way of your goal? Day seven hundred fifty-three.

Yudhishthira hears about Jarasandha and does something unexpected. He backs down. If even Krishna's people fled from this man, he says, how can we stand against him? Let's give up the sacrifice. Peace is better. It's a startling thing to hear from the man whose father asked for this. Then his brothers speak, one after the other. And then Krishna tells a story about how Jarasandha came to be born.
screen: `LET'S GIVE IT UP.` → `THE BROTHERS SPEAK.` → `KRISHNA TELLS A BIRTH STORY.`

segments.voice: Bhima speaks first, and bluntly. A king who never makes an effort, he says, gets worn down like an anthill. Then he offers a plan: Krishna's wisdom, my strength, Arjuna's skill. Together, the three of us can do this. Arjuna argues too: they have the strength and the weapons, he says, so why hold back? Yudhishthira's caution isn't mocked. It's answered. And then Krishna tells where Jarasandha came from. There was a king of Magadha named Brihadratha, with two wives and no son. A sage, Chandakaushika, gave him a single fruit to bring a son. The king divided it between his two wives, so that neither would be left out. Each queen gave birth to half a child. One eye, one arm, one leg each. Horrified, the queens had the halves left outside. A rakshasi named Jara found them, and as she picked them up, the halves joined into one strong child. She gave him back to the king. And the text says plainly that his name comes from her: Jarasandha, the one joined by Jara. Why tell this now, in a war council? The story slows down to show who the enemy is before anyone fights him. And it isn't only a monster's tale. A father who wouldn't leave either wife out. Two mothers who couldn't bear what they saw. A rakshasi who, instead of harming the child, carries him home. Even the enemy has a family story. Tomorrow, the three set out for Magadha, and they don't go dressed as warriors.
screen: `AN ANTHILL WEARS DOWN.` · `ONE FRUIT FOR TWO QUEENS.` · `TWO HALVES, JOINED BY JARA.` · `EVEN THE ENEMY HAS A FAMILY STORY.` · then, large: `THE ONE JOINED BY JARA.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go on its own. Bring to mind a time you wanted to give something up because it looked too big. Notice what helped, or would have helped: a plan, a friend, someone who saw your strengths more clearly than you did. Let that person or that plan come into view. If it's still in front of you, you might picture the next small step, just one. The bell holds the time.
The Rajasuya. Today, the sacrifice nearly given up, then taken back up, with a plan and a story about the enemy's birth.
Your line: the Rajasuya. Today, when someone wants to quit, answer their caution instead of mocking it. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: The story of Jarasandha's birth is told in the Sabha Parva of the Mahabharata, which Hindus read, hear recited and see performed as part of the epic.

fork.setup: you're King Brihadratha. a sage gives you one fruit for a son, and you have two wives. what do you do?
options: give it to the elder queen.
fork.reveal: he divides it so neither is left out. each queen bears half a child, and only Jara's touch makes them one.

original.note: Sanskrit jarāsandha: the text explains the name as 'joined by Jara', the rakshasi who joined his two halves.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monster's name.
what it means: a king born in two halves and joined into one by the rakshasi Jara.
what a scholar hears: the Mahabharata itself explains the name, from Jara, who joined the two halves into one child.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Rajasuyarambha and Jarasandha-vadha Parvas (Yudhishthira's hesitation; Bhima's and Arjuna's speeches; the birth of Jarasandha)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm Yudhishthira's wish to give up the sacrifice and his reasoning.
Confirm Bhima's anthill image (a king without exertion wasting like an anthill) and his plan of Krishna's policy, Bhima's strength and Arjuna's skill; confirm Arjuna's speech in substance.
Confirm birth details: Brihadratha, two wives, the sage Chandakaushika, a single fruit (mango) divided, half-bodies, Jara joining them, and the text's explanation of the name.
Retellings vary on how Bhima kills Jarasandha; this day avoids foreshadowing the manner of death.
howItsDone is general; a Keeper may wish to adjust it.
Audit: in Ganguli, Krishna speaks between Bhima and Arjuna, so the teach no longer says Arjuna simply "follows" Bhima.

Editor pass: hook no longer says the hall was 'built for exactly this kind of ambition' (Krishna asked Maya for a hall, not for ambition) or that Krishna told the birth story 'instead of arguing' (he also counsels before telling it).
